(i) in the presence of specific factors of production and/or urban unemployment the tariff induced capital inflow is not 'essentially' a function of the urban labor market conditions; (ii) in the presence and/or absence of specific factors of protection the tariff induced capital flow is not a'monotonic' function of the urban unemployment rate; and (iii) in the presence or absence of urban unemployment the tariff rate is not a'strictly monotonic' function of urban unemployment.

the tariff induced capital inflow is 'essentially' equal to the tariff induced capital outflow, that the tariff induced increase in the capital inflow is equal to the tariff imposed, and that the tariff induced reduction in the capital inflows is equal to the sum of the tariff imposed and the tariff induced capital reduction in the capital outflows.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the presence of urban unemployment, the tariff rate may induce capital inflows even if it does not induce capital inflows in the presence of full employment.
the Brecher's observation is not 'essentially' but rather 'comprehensively' valid in this setting.
the 'essential' result is not so essential after all.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a tariff may be welfare improving in the presence of capital inflows, even if the tariff reduces the wage rate and the level of employment in the urban sector, and even when the tariff is imposed by the developing country itself.
a country's ability to attract foreign investment in the face of a tariff is not necessarily a good thing for its economy.
, when the labor market in the urban sector is not perfectly competitive, tariff induced capital inflow can be associated with a decrease in welfare.
